'''John Lewis Tiarks''', FRS (born Johann Ludwig Tiarks, 10 May 1789 – 1 May 1837), '''Johann Ludwig Tiarks''', was a German mathematician who became the British astronomer to the [[Canada–United States border|North American Boundary Line Commission]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/><ref>{{cite journal|title= The Gentleman's Magazine |first = Sylvanus|last = Urban|year = 1838|page = 91}}{{failed verification|date=July 2026}}</ref>

==Early life==
He was born in Waddewarden, [[Wangerland]], [[Friesland (district)|Friesland]], [[Lower Saxony]] on 10 May 1789.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig>{{Cite web|url=http://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/tiarks_johann_ludwig_7E.html|title=TIARKS, JOHANN LUDWIG|access-date=2020-09-11|website=[[Dictionary of Canadian Biography]]}}</ref> His father was Reverend Johann Gerhard Tiarks and his mother was Christine Dorothea Ehrentraut.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>

He entered the [[University of Göttingen]] to study theology but transferred to the mathematics course. He took a position as a private [[tutor]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> He received a doctorate in mathematics in 1808.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> Having gained his degree he initially moved to [[Hamburg]]. He fled to [[England]] in 1810 to avoid [[conscription]] by [[Napoleon]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> He became assistant librarian and factotum to [[Joseph Banks]] at the [[Royal Society]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>

==First visit to North America==
In 1817, on Banks’ recommendation, he was appointed an astronomer to one of the commissions established under the [[Treaty of Ghent]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> He acted for [[Joseph Bouchette]] who fell ill that year.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> He remained with the commission after Bouchette was replaced with [[William Franklin Odell]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> In September 1817 he arrived in [[Akwesasne]] to make astronomical observations.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> He befriended many of the local [[Mohawk people]] and their priest, Father Joseph Marcoux.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> 

At the end of July 1818 Tiarks and his group left Akwesasne and with the American surveying team headed to [[Lake Champlain]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> [[Ferdinand Rudolph Hassler]] headed the American team.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> At the lake both teams independently discovered that [[John Collins (merchant)|John Collins]] and others had incorrectly located the [[45th parallel north]], placing the fort at [[Rouses Point, New York]] in British territory.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> The American members of the boundary commission refused to accept the findings.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> Hassler had been replaced as astronomer by [[Andrew Ellicott]], who was far less cooperative.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> Ellicott was reported as saying to Tiarks "we should not do our work so exactingly and forget about completing most of it".<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> Tiarks refused to go along with the suggestion, as he felt it put his reputation on the line.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> He was strongly supported in this by British Commissioner [[Thomas Henry Barclay]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> 

In 1819 he was working in the upper [[Connecticut River]] basin where part of the boundary was to run.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> During summer 1820 he was working in what became northwestern [[New Brunswick]] and nearby areas of [[Quebec]], returning to the upper Connecticut that fall.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> Disputes between British and American commissioners brought his work to a halt and he returned to Europe in 1821.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>

==Europe==
Due to delays in proceeding with the border project, the [[British Admiralty]] asked him in the meantime to determine the longitude of various European locations, such as Madeira, with the help of chronometers, for which the ''[[HMS Comet (1822)|SS Comet]]'' had been specially outfitted. He was joined from 30 June to 17 August 1824 by [[Humphry Davy]] who used the voyage to [[Norway]] to test his [[Cathodic protection|zinc protectors]] for ships' bottoms.<ref>'''The Royal Society, MC. 1. 114'''</ref> In 1825 Tiarks was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] as "a person well versed in mathematics and nautical astronomy".<ref>{{cite web|url= https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Persons&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28%28text%29%3D%27tiarks%27%29|title= Fellows Details|publisher= Royal Society|accessdate= 19 April 2015}}{{Dead link|date=November 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Second visit to North America==
{{main|Northwesternmost point of the Lake of the Woods}}
He returned to North America in 1825 to determine the northwestermost point of the [[Lake of the Woods]], from which the boundary was supposed to run due west to the [[Mississippi River]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> 

From 1826 to 1830 he worked on matters of concern to the boundary commission.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>  He was called to [[The Hague]] to explain certain points to [[William II of the Netherlands]], who had been asked to arbitrate the boundary question.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> Tiarks returned to Jeven.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>

==Personal life==
In 1822 he married Auguste Antoinette Sophie Toel of [[Jever]].<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/> They had several children, but only one daughter survived to adulthood.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>

==Final years and death==
He long wished to be a professor in a German university, but no position ever became available. In March 1837 he suffered from a [[stroke]] from which he never recovered.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>

The [[Webster–Ashburton Treaty]], which settled the boundary disputes in question, was signed in 1842.<ref name=dict-canadian-bio-tiarks-johann-ludwig/>
